claim: Phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP) is a key intermediate in the biosynthesis of purine and pyrimidine nucleotides, histidine, tryptophan, and cofactors NAD and NADP.
source: Phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP) is a key intermediate in the biosynthesis of purine and pyrimidine nucleotides, histidine, tryptophan, and cofactors NAD and NADP.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature (Hove-Jensen, 1988; Munch-Petersen, 1983) in the manuscript.

claim: Abnormal regulation of PRPP synthase (PRPS) is associated with human disorders, including Arts syndrome, retinal dystrophy, and gouty arthritis.
source: Abnormal regulation of PRPP synthase (PRPS) is associated with human disorders, including Arts syndrome, retinal dystrophy, and gouty arthritis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations in the manuscript to prior research on PRPS-related disorders.

claim: PRPS can form filamentous cytoophidia in eukaryotes.
source: Recent studies have demonstrated that PRPS can form filamentous cytoophidia in eukaryotes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies in the manuscript.

claim: PRPS forms cytoophidia in prokaryotes both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Here, we show that PRPS forms cytoophidia in prokaryotes both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including negative staining EM and fluorescence microscopy.

claim: Two distinct filament structures of E. coli PRPS were solved at near-atomic resolution using Cryo-EM.
source: Moreover, we solve two distinct filament structures of E. coli PRPS at near-atomic resolution using Cryo-EM.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM data and structural models presented in the manuscript.

claim: The formation of the two types of filaments is controlled by the binding of different ligands.
source: The formation of the two types of filaments is controlled by the binding of different ligands.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing different filament types form under different ligand conditions.

claim: One filament type is resistant to allosteric inhibition.
source: One filament type is resistant to allosteric inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by biochemical activity assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Conformational changes of a regulatory flexible loop may regulate the binding of the allosteric inhibitor and the substrate ATP.
source: The structural comparison reveals conformational changes of a regulatory flexible loop, which may regulate the binding of the allosteric inhibitor and the substrate ATP.
evidence: This claim is based on structural comparisons and inference from the cryo-EM structures.

claim: A noncanonical allosteric AMP/ADP binding site is identified to stabilize the conformation of the regulatory flexible loop.
source: A noncanonical allosteric AMP/ADP binding site is identified to stabilize the conformation of the regulatory flexible loop.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data showing AMP/ADP binding at a novel site.

claim: PRPP is synthesized by PRPS, which catalyzes the transfer of diphosphate from ATP to ribose-5-phosphate (R5P), thereby generating AMP and PRPP.
source: PRPP is synthesized by PRPP synthase (PRPS), which catalyzes the transfer of diphosphate from ATP to ribose-5-phosphate (R5P), thereby generating AMP and PRPP (Khorana et al., 1958).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Missense mutations of PRPS1 alter enzyme activity or allosteric regulation and are associated with severe pathological outcomes.
source: In humans, missense mutations of PRPP synthase isozyme 1 (PRPS1) alter enzyme activity or the allosteric regulation and are associated with many severe pathological outcomes (Becker et al., 1995; Chen et al., 2013; Duley et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Decreased activity of PRPS1 may result in neurological disorders, such as Arts syndrome, non-syndromic sensorineural deafness 2 (DFN2), Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease 5 (CMTX5), and retinal dystrophy.
source: The decreased activity of this enzyme may result in neurological disorders, such as Arts syndrome, non-syndromic sensorineural deafness 2 (DFN2), Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease 5 (CMTX5), and retinal dystrophy.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Hyperactivity of PRPS1 may lead to neurosensory defects, hyperuricemia, or gouty arthritis.
source: Conversely, hyperactivity of PRPS1 may lead to neurosensory defects, hyperuricemia, or gouty arthritis.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Dysregulation of PRPS1 or PRPS2 activity and expression has been observed in many cancers and is associated with thiopurine resistance in recurrent childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
source: Dysregulation of PRPS1 or PRPS2 activity and expression has been observed in many cancers and is associated with thiopurine resistance in recurrent childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Cunningham et al., 2014; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Class I PRPP synthase is the most widely distributed in phylogeny, including E. coli and humans.
source: Class I PRPP synthase is the most widely distributed in phylogeny, including E. coli and humans.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of PRPS classification.

claim: Phosphate ion (Pi) is necessary to activate class I PRPS.
source: Phosphate ion (Pi) is necessary to activate class I PRPS, while ADP, an allosteric inhibitor, competes with Pi and ATP at allosteric and active sites, respectively (Eriksen et al., 2000; Hove-Jensen et al., 1986; Nosal et al., 1993; Willemoës et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: ADP, an allosteric inhibitor, competes with Pi and ATP at allosteric and active sites, respectively.
source: Phosphate ion (Pi) is necessary to activate class I PRPS, while ADP, an allosteric inhibitor, competes with Pi and ATP at allosteric and active sites, respectively (Eriksen et al., 2000; Hove-Jensen et al., 1986; Nosal et al., 1993; Willemoës et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Class II PRPS is active without Pi.
source: However, class II PRPS is active without Pi.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: ADP does not bind to the allosteric site of the class II PRPS but inhibits it competitively.
source: ADP does not bind to the allosteric site of the class II PRPS but inhibits it competitively (Krath et al., 1999; Krath and Hove-Jensen, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Class III PRPS present in archaea requires Pi to activate, but there is no allosteric mechanism.
source: Class III PRPS present in archaea requires Pi to activate, but there is no allosteric mechanism (Kadziola et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: PRPS cytoophidia have been identified in various eukaryotes, including budding yeast, fruit flies, zebrafish, and mammals.
source: Recently, PRPS has been identified as a novel cytoophidium-forming enzyme in various eukaryotes, including budding yeast, fruit flies, zebrafish, and mammals (Begovich et al., 2020; Noree et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent research.

claim: E. coli PRPS has 47.5% sequence identity to human PRPS1 and PRPS2.
source: There is only one PRPS gene in E. coli genome, which has 47.5% sequence identity to human PRPS1 and PRPS2 (Tatibana et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: When PRPS was incubated without ligands, no filaments were found.
source: When PRPS was incubated without ligands, no filaments were found, indicating that E. coli PRPS was not easy to polymerize.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations using negative staining EM.

claim: PRPS filaments were not found with only AMP (2 mM).
source: PRPS filaments were also not found with only AMP (2 mM).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations using negative staining EM.

claim: When PRPS was incubated with ATP or any adenine nucleotide and Mg2+ (10 mM), many PRPS filaments could be observed.
source: However, when PRPS was incubated only with ATP or any adenine nucleotide and Mg2+ (10 mM), many PRPS filaments could be observed.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations using negative staining EM.

claim: PRPS filamentated at 50 mM Pi.
source: On the other hand, we also incubated PRPS at Pi concentrations of 10, 30, and 50 mM, and found that PRPS filamentated at 50 mM Pi (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The twist and rise of type A filament are 27° (left-handed twist) and 63 Å, respectively.
source: The twist and rise of type A filament are 27° (left-handed twist) and 63 Å, respectively, and the twist and rise of type B are 46° (left-handed twist) and 66 Å, respectively (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: The twist and rise of type B filament are 46° (left-handed twist) and 66 Å, respectively.
source: The twist and rise of type A filament are 27° (left-handed twist) and 63 Å, respectively, and the twist and rise of type B are 46° (left-handed twist) and 66 Å, respectively (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: In type A filament, R5P was found at the active site.
source: Surprisingly, in type A filament, we found R5P at the active site, and the ATP binding site was occupied by ADP rather than ATP.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis.

claim: In type A filament, the ATP binding site was occupied by ADP rather than ATP.
source: Surprisingly, in type A filament, we found R5P at the active site, and the ATP binding site was occupied by ADP rather than ATP.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis.

claim: In type A filament, another ADP is located at a noncanonical binding site (allosteric site 2).
source: In addition, another ADP is located at a noncanonical binding site (allosteric site 2), which is bound by AMP in the Legionella pneumophila PRPS structure (PDB ID: 6NFE), while Pi is located at the binding position of the β-phosphate of ADP at the canonical ADP allosteric site (allosteric site 1) (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis and comparison with other structures.

claim: Pi is located at the binding position of the β-phosphate of ADP at the canonical ADP allosteric site (allosteric site 1) in type A filament.
source: In addition, another ADP is located at a noncanonical binding site (allosteric site 2), which is bound by AMP in the Legionella pneumophila PRPS structure (PDB ID: 6NFE), while Pi is located at the binding position of the β-phosphate of ADP at the canonical ADP allosteric site (allosteric site 1) (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis.

claim: ADP in the type A filament model might come from the spontaneous hydrolysis of ATP or be preserved during protein purification.
source: Since we did not add ADP to the mixture for sample preparation, ADP in the model might come from the spontaneous hydrolysis of ATP or be preserved during protein purification.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental conditions.

claim: In type B filament, R5P binding site and allosteric site 1 are bound by Pi.
source: Meanwhile, in type B filament, R5P binding site and allosteric site 1 are bound by Pi, while ATP binding site and allosteric site 2 are empty (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In type B filament, ATP binding site and allosteric site 2 are empty.
source: Meanwhile, in type B filament, R5P binding site and allosteric site 1 are bound by Pi, while ATP binding site and allosteric site 2 are empty (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The PRPS monomers in type A and type B filaments are highly similar except for the regulatory flexible loop region (RF loop, Y94 to T109).
source: The structural comparison between the two models shows that the PRPS monomers in type A and type B filaments are highly similar except for the regulatory flexible loop region (RF loop, Y94 to T109) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The 5.2° rotation of hexamer leads to closed (type A) and open (type B) conformations.
source: The main difference between the hexamers in the two filaments lies in the relative position of the monomers in the parallel dimer. The 5.2° rotation of hexamer leads to closed (type A) and open (type B) conformations (Figure 2B–D, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: In the type A filament model, R5P and ADP at the active site are in association with two Mg2+.
source: In the type A filament model, R5P and ADP at the active site are in association with two Mg2+.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis.

claim: One Mg2+ (Mg site 1) coordinates the C1, C2, and C3 hydroxyl groups of R5P with D170 and two water molecules.
source: One Mg2+ (Mg site 1) coordinates the C1, C2, and C3 hydroxyl groups of R5P with D170 and two water molecules, and the other Mg2+ (Mg site 2) coordinates oxygens of the α- and β-phosphates of ADP (active site) with H131 and three water molecules (Figure 3A and B, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The other Mg2+ (Mg site 2) coordinates oxygens of the α- and β-phosphates of ADP (active site) with H131 and three water molecules.
source: One Mg2+ (Mg site 1) coordinates the C1, C2, and C3 hydroxyl groups of R5P with D170 and two water molecules, and the other Mg2+ (Mg site 2) coordinates oxygens of the α- and β-phosphates of ADP (active site) with H131 and three water molecules (Figure 3A and B, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The ADP at the active site of chain B forms hydrogen bonds with D37 in chain C.
source: The ADP at the active site of chain B forms hydrogen bonds with D37 in chain C, and there is a π-π interaction between F35 in chain C and adenine base.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis.

claim: There is a π-π interaction between F35 in chain C and adenine base of ADP at the active site.
source: The ADP at the active site of chain B forms hydrogen bonds with D37 in chain C, and there is a π-π interaction between F35 in chain C and adenine base.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis.

claim: R99 and H131 in chain B form salt bridges with the β and α-phosphate of ADP at the active site, respectively.
source: R99 and H131 in chain B form salt bridges with the β and α-phosphate, respectively (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: The α-phosphate of the ADP also interacts with R5P through hydrogen bonds with the C-1 hydroxyl group.
source: The α-phosphate of the ADP also interacts with R5P through hydrogen bonds with the C-1 hydroxyl group.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis.

claim: R5P of chain B forms hydrogen bonds with D170, D220, D221, T225, and T228 in the same chain.
source: R5P of chain B forms hydrogen bonds with D170, D220, D221, T225, and T228 in the same chain (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: ADP binds allosteric site 2 in chain A through hydrogen bonding with R102 in chain B, and S149, E133 in chain A.
source: ADP binds allosteric site 2 in chain A through hydrogen bonding with R102 in chain B, and S149, E133 in chain A, and a π-π interaction between F147 of chain A and adenine bases, and salt bridges between R102 in chain B, R178 in chain A, and phosphates (Figure 3D, Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There is a π-π interaction between F147 of chain A and adenine bases of ADP at allosteric site 2.
source: ADP binds allosteric site 2 in chain A through hydrogen bonding with R102 in chain B, and S149, E133 in chain A, and a π-π interaction between F147 of chain A and adenine bases, and salt bridges between R102 in chain B, R178 in chain A, and phosphates (Figure 3D, Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Salt bridges form between R102 in chain B, R178 in chain A, and phosphates of ADP at allosteric site 2.
source: ADP binds allosteric site 2 in chain A through hydrogen bonding with R102 in chain B, and S149, E133 in chain A, and a π-π interaction between F147 of chain A and adenine bases, and salt bridges between R102 in chain B, R178 in chain A, and phosphates (Figure 3D, Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Allosteric site 2 binds to AMP in Legionella pneumophila PRPS structure (PDB ID: 6NFE).
source: Allosteric site 2 binds to AMP in Legionella pneumophila PRPS structure (PDB ID: 6NFE), which is adjacent to allosteric site 2 bound with SO42+ in multiple human PRPS1 structures (PDB ID: 2H06 and 2HCR) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a published structure.

claim: A type AAMP/ADP filament was solved, which was formed under the conditions of AMP (2 mM)+ADP (2 mM).
source: Parallel to the above two structures, we also solved another type A filament (type AAMP/ADP), which was formed under the conditions of AMP (2 mM)+ADP (2 mM) (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The type AAMP/ADP structure is almost the same as the former type A filament model, but its allosteric site 2 is bound by AMP rather than ADP.
source: This structure is almost the same as the former type A filament model, but its allosteric site 2 is bound by AMP rather than ADP (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The allosteric site 1 in type AAMP/ADP model is empty.
source: In addition, the allosteric site 1 in type AAMP/ADP model is empty, supporting that the presence of ADP and Pi in the former type A filament model were due to spontaneous hydrolysis of ATP.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis.

claim: The allosteric site 2 of E. coli PRPS may accommodate both AMP and ADP.
source: According to our two type A filament models, the allosteric site 2 of E. coli PRPS may accommodate both AMP and ADP.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the two type A filament structures.

claim: In the model of type B filament, allosteric site 1 is bound by Pi and allosteric site 2 is incomplete due to the conformational change of hexamer from closed to open.
source: In the model of type B filament, allosteric site 1 is bound by Pi and allosteric site 2 is incomplete due to the conformational change of hexamer from closed to open (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: The 5-phosphate of R5P on the active site is replaced by Pi in type B filament.
source: The 5-phosphate of R5P on the active site is replaced by Pi (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The ATP binding site in the active site of type B filament is not bound by the ligand, but occupied by the RF loop.
source: Intriguingly, our density map shows that the ATP binding site in the active site is not bound by the ligand, but occupied by the RF loop (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The B-factor of the RF loop in the type B filament ranges from 50.5 to 93.3 Å2, indicating its flexibility.
source: The B-factor of the RF loop in the type B filament ranges from 50.5 to 93.3 Å2, indicating its flexibility (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In type A filaments, the RF loop is stabilized by a variety of interactions, including the salt bridge between R102 and α-phosphate of ADP at allosteric site 2, resulting in smaller B factors ranges from 29.4 to 44.5 Å2.
source: However, in type A filaments, the RF loop is stabilized by a variety of interactions, including the salt bridge between R102 and α-phosphate of ADP at allosteric site 2, resulting in smaller B factors ranges from 29.4 to 44.5 Å2 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The RF loop in type A filament is stabilized at a conformation and covers the ADP binding pocket at allosteric site 1.
source: On the other hand, the RF loop in type A filament is stabilized at a conformation and covers the ADP binding pocket at allosteric site 1.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis.

claim: The conformation of the RF loop in type A filament results in the closure of allosteric site 1, thereby preventing the binding of allosteric inhibitor ADP.
source: This conformation results in the closure of allosteric site 1, thereby preventing the binding of allosteric inhibitor ADP (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the structural data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In type A filaments, hexamers are connected by salt bridges formed between R301 and E298 pairs, by the hydrogen bonds between R301, N305, and E307, and also by van der Waals force between R302 and R301.
source: In type A filaments, hexamers are connected by salt bridges formed between R301 and E298 pairs, by the hydrogen bonds between R301, N305, and E307, and also by van der Waals force between R302 and R301 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In the type B filament, the connection between hexamers relies on the π-cation interaction between Y24 and R22, and the hydrogen bond between R301 and L23.
source: In the type B filament, the connection between hexamers relies on the π-cation interaction between Y24 and R22, and the hydrogen bond between R301 and L23 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: PRPSR302A/Y24A failed to assemble filaments under all conditions.
source: As expected, PRPSR302A/Y24A failed to assemble filaments under all conditions, and PRPSR302A and PRPSY24A could only form type B and type A filaments, respectively (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A using negative staining EM.

claim: PRPSR302A could only form type B filaments.
source: As expected, PRPSR302A/Y24A failed to assemble filaments under all conditions, and PRPSR302A and PRPSY24A could only form type B and type A filaments, respectively (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A using negative staining EM.

claim: PRPSY24A could only form type A filaments.
source: As expected, PRPSR302A/Y24A failed to assemble filaments under all conditions, and PRPSR302A and PRPSY24A could only form type B and type A filaments, respectively (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A using negative staining EM.

claim: In the absence of ADP, the activity of PRPSR302A decreased significantly, while the activity of PRPSR302A/Y24R was higher.
source: In the absence of ADP, the activity of PRPSR302A decreased significantly, while the activity of PRPSR302A/Y24R was higher (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by biochemical activity assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: When ADP (0.1 mM) was added into the mixture, the activity of PRPSR302A and PRPSR302A/Y24A dropped dramatically by 82.3% and 85.1% respectively, whereas the activities of PRPSWT and PRPSY24A decreased only by 37.8% and 18.9%, respectively.
source: When ADP (0.1 mM) was added into the mixture, the activity of PRPSR302A and PRPSR302A/Y24A dropped dramatically by 82.3% and 85.1% respectively, whereas the activities of PRPSWT and PRPSY24A decreased only by 37.8% and 18.9%, respectively (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by biochemical activity assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: When ADP (0.1 mM) was supplied at 2 mM ATP, the activity of PRPSWT and PRPSR302A dropped by 32.2% and 91.6%, respectively.
source: When ADP (0.1 mM) was supplied, activity deceased in most groups (Figure 6C). The activity of PRPSWT and PRPSR302A dropped by 32.2% and 91.6%, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by biochemical activity assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The activity of PRPSY24A has not changed when ADP (0.1 mM) was supplied at 2 mM ATP, indicating that the absence of type B filament leads to significant resistance to allosteric inhibition.
source: The only exception is PRPSY24A, whose activity has not changed, indicating that the absence of type B filament leads to significant resistance to allosteric inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by biochemical activity assay data and inference from the results.

claim: After adding ADP, the activity of PRPSR302A/Y24R decreased by 55.4%, indicating that filamentation is not required for allosteric inhibition.
source: After adding ADP, the activity of PRPSR302A/Y24R decreased by 55.4%, indicating that filamentation is not required for allosteric inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by biochemical activity assay data and inference from the results.

claim: Polymerization significantly affects the activity of PRPS under in vitro conditions.
source: Although it is unlikely that all PRPS were within filaments during the measurement, these results still show that polymerization significantly affects the activity of PRPS under these in vitro conditions.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the biochemical activity assay data.

claim: When ATP was 0.6 mM, the activity of PRPSE133A was four times lower than that of PRPSWT.
source: Therefore, we intended to impair the interaction between the C2 hydroxyl group of ADP and the side chain of E133 by introducing the point mutation E133A. As expected, when ATP was 0.6 mM, the activity of PRPSE133A was four times lower than that of PRPSWT.
evidence: This claim is supported by biochemical activity assay data.

claim: When ATP was increased to 2 mM, the activity of PRPSE133A increased to a level comparable to that of PRPSWT.
source: However, when ATP was increased to 2 mM, the activity of PRPSE133A increased to a level comparable to that of PRPSWT.
evidence: This claim is supported by biochemical activity assay data.

claim: Corresponding human PRPS1S132A mutant also displayed reduced activity in a previous study.
source: Corresponding human PRPS1S132A mutant also displayed reduced activity in a previous study (Li et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: AMP/ADP at allosteric site 2 may facilitate the binding of ATP at the active site.
source: These results suggest that AMP/ADP at allosteric site 2 may facilitate the binding of ATP at the active site (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the biochemical activity assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In a small subset of cells (less than 1%), filamentous structures of PRPSWT-mCherry could be observed.
source: In a small subset of cells (less than 1%), filamentous structures of PRPSWT-mCherry could be observed (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: PRPSR302A-mCherry filaments and punctate aggregates were observed in about 1% cells.
source: In contrast, PRPSR302A-mCherry filaments and punctate aggregates were observed in about 1% cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: In cells expressing PRPSY24A-mCherry, filaments were not found, but punctate aggregates were observed less than 1% cells.
source: In cells expressing PRPSY24A-mCherry, filaments were not found, but punctate aggregates were observed less than 1% cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: At all stages of growth, no filaments or punctate aggregates were observed in cells expressing PRPSR302A/Y24A-mCherry.
source: At all stages of growth, no filaments or punctate aggregates were observed in cells expressing PRPSR302A/Y24A-mCherry.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data.

claim: The growth rate of cells overexpressing PRPSWT, PRPSR302A, and PRPSY24A was significantly faster than that of wild-type Transetta cells.
source: The growth rate of cells overexpressing PRPSWT, PRPSR302A, and PRPSY24A was significantly faster than that of wild-type Transetta cells, while the growth rate of cells overexpressing PRPSR302A/Y24A was similar to that of wild-type cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The growth rate of cells overexpressing PRPSR302A/Y24A was similar to that of wild-type cells.
source: The growth rate of cells overexpressing PRPSWT, PRPSR302A, and PRPSY24A was significantly faster than that of wild-type Transetta cells, while the growth rate of cells overexpressing PRPSR302A/Y24A was similar to that of wild-type cells (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Both type A and type B PRPS filaments exist in vivo.
source: Although we cannot rule out the unexpected effects of PRPS overexpression and mCherry tagging, our results show that both type A and type B PRPS filaments exist in vivo.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the fluorescence microscopy and growth curve data.

claim: Between E. coli and human PRPS1/2, the hexameric propeller structure of PRPS and the identified residues responsible for polymerization are conserved.
source: Between E. coli and human PRPS1/2, the hexameric propeller structure of PRPS and the identified residues responsible for polymerization are conserved, indicating that type A and / or type B PRPS filaments may also exist in mammals.
evidence: This claim is based on structural comparison and inference.

claim: Type A and/or type B PRPS filaments may also exist in mammals.
source: Between E. coli and human PRPS1/2, the hexameric propeller structure of PRPS and the identified residues responsible for polymerization are conserved, indicating that type A and / or type B PRPS filaments may also exist in mammals.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on structural conservation.

claim: PRPS isolated from rat liver tissues revealed a heterogenous protein complex with a molecular weight greater than 1000 kDa.
source: In fact, PRPS isolated from rat liver tissues revealed a heterogenous protein complex with a molecular weight greater than 1000 kDa (Kita et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: A similar phenomenon was observed in human PRPS1/2 isolated from tissue sources.
source: A similar phenomenon was observed in human PRPS1/2 isolated from tissue sources (Becker et al., 1977; Fox and Kelley, 1971).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

source: This mechanism provides a new PRPS regulatory layer that can fine tune the production of PRPP and coordinate cellular metabolic pathways.

claim: ADP is an effective PRPS inhibitor because it can reduce the activity of rat PRPS by about 40~50% at a concentration of 0.1 mM.
source: ADP is an effective PRPS inhibitor because it can reduce the activity of rat PRPS by about 40~50% at a concentration of 0.1 mM (Tatibana et al., 1995).

source: Consistent with previous studies (Willemoës et al., 2000), we showed that when 0.1 mM ADP was added into the reaction mixture, the PRPSWT activity of E. coli decreased by about 40% (Figure 6B and C).

claim: Allosteric inhibition by ADP could be compromised by the formation of type A filaments.
source: However, we show that this allosteric inhibition by ADP could be compromised by the formation of type A filaments (Figure 6B).

source: In this model, the RF loop moves toward allosteric site 1, thereby enclosing the ADP binding pocket.

source: A similar mechanism has been depicted in a previous report on human PRPS1 crystal structures, in which the adjacent allosteric site 2 is bound by SO42- (Li et al., 2007).

claim: PRPS filamentation is not essential for the regulatory function of allosteric site 2, but could enhance such an effect.

claim: Intracellular ADP level is generally within the range of hundreds micromolar in E. coli and mammalian cells.
source: Since intracellular ADP level is generally within the range of hundreds micromolar in E. coli and mammalian cells (Meyrat and von Ballmoos, 2019; Traut, 1994), it is reasonable to propose that type A filament facilitates PRPP production in cells (Traut, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Type A filament facilitates PRPP production in cells.

claim: AMP/ADP at allosteric site 2 interacts with the RF loop, thereby stabilizing the loop at allosteric site 1.
source: In our type A filament model, additional allosteric site 2 binds to AMP/ADP (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1). AMP/ADP at this binding site interacts with the RF loop, thereby stabilizing the loop at allosteric site 1.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Allosteric site 2 is incomplete in the PRPS open hexamer (type B filament) and cannot bind to AMP/ADP, resulting in an unstable RF loop.
source: In contrast, allosteric site 2 is incomplete in the PRPS open hexamer (type B filament) and cannot bind to AMP/ADP, resulting in an unstable RF loop (Figure 4A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from cryo-EM analysis shown in Figure 4A and C.

claim: The point mutation E133A is expected to impair allosteric site 2, resulting in a significant decrease in activity.
source: The point mutation E133A is expected to impair allosteric site 2, resulting in a significant decrease in activity, which supports our hypothesis about the function of allosteric site 2.
evidence: This claim is supported by biochemical activity assay data.

claim: Certain point mutations may be applicable to industry.

source: Moreover, PRPS, as the upstream enzyme of CTPS and IMPDH, indicates that the regulation of enzyme function through filamentation is particularly important for de novo nucleotide biosynthesis.
